summary: Insulin glargine is a long-acting human insulin analog given subcutaneously once daily to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes and in adults with type 2 diabetes. It provides a slow, relatively peakless basal insulin effect lasting about 24 hours. It must not be used for diabetic ketoacidosis and must not be diluted or mixed with other insulins. The main risks are hypoglycemia and hypokalemia; dosing is individualized and changes in insulin regimen require close glucose monitoring.
indications: Improvement of glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus
Improvement of glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

moa: The primary activity of insulin glargine is regulation of glucose metabolism. It lowers blood glucose by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake, especially by skeletal muscle and fat, and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. It also inhibits lipolysis and proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. After subcutaneous injection the acidic solution is neutralized, forming microprecipitates that release insulin slowly, producing a prolonged, relatively peakless effect.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to insulin glargine or any excipient
relative: Diabetic ketoacidosis (not recommended; use rapid-acting IV insulin)
monitor: Blood glucose, especially with regimen changes
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hypokalemia
Signs of hypoglycemia, particularly with hypoglycemia unawareness

preg: Published studies of insulin glargine in pregnancy have not shown a clear association with adverse developmental outcomes; poorly controlled diabetes itself carries substantial maternal and fetal risk. Insulin glargine can be used in pregnancy with careful glucose management.
lact: Insulin glargine is compatible with breastfeeding; insulin is a large protein that is not orally absorbed by the nursing infant. Lactating women may require dose adjustment and meal modification.
renal: Insulin requirements may be reduced in renal impairment due to decreased insulin clearance; monitor glucose closely and adjust the dose to avoid hypoglycemia.
hepatic: Insulin requirements may be reduced in hepatic impairment due to reduced gluconeogenesis and altered insulin metabolism; monitor glucose closely and adjust the dose.

major: Drugs increasing hypoglycemia risk: other antidiabetics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, disopyramide, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAOIs, pentoxifylline, pramlintide, salicylates, somatostatin analogs, sulfonamide antibiotics (reduce insulin dose; monitor glucose)
moderate: Drugs decreasing glucose-lowering effect: atypical antipsychotics, corticosteroids, danazol, diuretics, estrogens/oral contraceptives, glucagon, isoniazid, niacin, phenothiazines, progestogens, protease inhibitors, somatropin, sympathomimetics, thyroid hormones (may need higher dose)
Thiazolidinediones (fluid retention, risk of heart failure)
interactions.food: Not meal-dependent as a basal insulin; consistent carbohydrate intake aids glucose control.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol, beta-blockers, clonidine, and lithium may increase or decrease the glucose-lowering effect; alcohol and beta-blockers may also mask or prolong hypoglycemia.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause hypokalemia; monitor potassium in at-risk patients.

common: Lipodystrophy / cutaneous amyloidosis at injection sites
serious: Fluid retention and heart failure (with TZDs)

counsel: Inject once daily at the same time each day; never inject into a vein
Rotate injection sites within the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm to protect your skin
Do not mix or dilute glargine with any other insulin
Recognize and treat low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) with fast-acting sugar; carry glucose
Never share your insulin pen with anyone, even with a new needle; store unused pens in the refrigerator
pk: Gradual; effect develops over several hours after SC injection
Effective duration governs dosing rather than a discrete half-life
Unused: refrigerate 2-8 C (do not freeze). In-use pen: room temperature up to 28 days per labeling; protect from heat and light
pearls: Basal, relatively peakless ~24-hour insulin; usually combined with prandial insulin in type 1 diabetes
Never use for DKA and never give IV; subcutaneous only
Do not dilute or mix with other insulins
Insulin needs often fall in renal or hepatic impairment; monitor for hypoglycemia
missed: If a basal dose is missed, contact your healthcare provider for advice; do not take a double dose. Resume the usual once-daily schedule and monitor blood glucose closely.
overdose: Excess insulin relative to food intake or activity causes severe, sometimes prolonged hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. Treat mild hypoglycemia with oral glucose; treat severe episodes (coma, seizure, neurologic impairment) with glucagon or IV glucose, sustain carbohydrate intake, and observe for recurrence. Correct hypokalemia.
